title: Group By
statement:
Give every array a method `groupBy(fn)`. Calling `array.groupBy(fn)` sorts the elements of `array` into groups and returns them as an object: `fn(item)` turns each element into a string key, and the object has one property per distinct key, holding the list of all elements that produced that key. Inside each list the elements keep their order from `array`; the properties themselves may come in any order. An empty array gives `{}`. The method belongs on `Array.prototype` so that every array has it, and it must be written by hand, without `Object.groupBy` or lodash's `_.groupBy`.

A case is JSON, so `fn` is given as one of these descriptions, which the judge turns into the real function:

- `"string"`: `String(item)`.
- `{ "get": k }`: `String(item[k])`, the property or index `k` of the element as a string (`"undefined"` when it is missing).
- `{ "greaterThan": v }`: `String(item > v)`, so `"true"` or `"false"`.
- `{ "mod": m }`: `String(item % m)`.

The judge calls `array.groupBy(fn)` once and answers with the object it returns, its keys listed in sorted order.
constraints: array is a valid JSON array
fn is "string", { "get": k }, { "greaterThan": v } or { "mod": m } with m a non-zero integer
With get, every element is an object or an array; with greaterThan and mod, every element is a number
fn returns a string for every element, and never "__proto__"
api: interface Array<T> { groupBy(fn: (item: T) => string): Record<string, T[]> }
notes:
## Intuition

Every array inherits from `Array.prototype`, so a function stored there becomes a method of every array, and inside it `this` is the array it was called on. Grouping then takes one pass: compute each element's key and append the element to that key's list, creating the list the first time the key shows up. Appending in array order keeps each list in the original order for free. The lists are collected in a `Map`, which holds only the keys put into it, and `Object.fromEntries` turns it into the plain object the problem asks for at the end. (The brute force first computes all keys, then, for each distinct key, filters the whole array again: correct, but O(n · number of keys).)

## Approach

1. Assign a regular `function` (not an arrow function) to `Array.prototype.groupBy`, so `this` is the array.
2. Start with an empty map `groups = new Map()`.
3. For each `item` of `this`, compute `key = fn(item)`.
4. If `groups.has(key)` is false, add the key with a new empty list: `groups.set(key, [])`.
5. Push `item` onto `groups.get(key)`.
6. After the loop, return `Object.fromEntries(groups)`: one property per key, holding that key's list.

## Example 1, step by step

`array = [{id: "1"}, {id: "1"}, {id: "2"}]` and `fn` reads `id`.

- First item: `key = "1"`, which `groups` lacks, so `groups.set("1", [])`; push the item.
- Second item: `key = "1"` is already in `groups`; push it, so `groups.get("1")` holds two items.
- Third item: `key = "2"` is new; set its empty list and push.
- `Object.fromEntries(groups)` returns `{ "1": [{id: "1"}, {id: "1"}], "2": [{id: "2"}] }`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one call of `fn` and O(1) average map work per element, plus one pass over the keys in `Object.fromEntries`.
- Space: O(n) for the lists, which together hold every element once.

## Pitfalls

- With an arrow function, `this` is not the array.
- Grouping straight into a plain object breaks on inherited names: `groups[key] ||= []` finds the inherited function for a key like `"toString"` or `"constructor"`, so no list is created and `push` fails, and even after an own-property check `groups["__proto__"] = []` replaces the prototype instead of adding a key. A `Map` has no inherited keys, and `Object.fromEntries` makes every key an own property.
- Calling `fn` twice per element (once to test, once to store) is wasteful; compute the key once.
- Sorting or reversing the lists: each group must keep the elements' original order.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `this` | the array that `groupBy` was called on |
| `fn` | turns an element into its string key |
| `groups` | map from each key to the list of the elements with that key, returned as a plain object |
| `item` | the current element |
| `key` | `fn(item)`, the group `item` belongs to |

narration.1: Store a regular function on Array.prototype so every array gets groupBy and this is that array.
narration.2: groups is a map from each key to the list of elements that produced it.
narration.3: Visit the elements in array order, which keeps every group in that order too.
narration.4: Ask fn which group this element belongs to, once per element.
narration.5: Is this the first element with this key? A map holds only the keys set on it, so keys like "toString" are safe.
narration.6: Start an empty list for the new key.
narration.8: Get the key's list and append the element to it.
narration.10: Every element has been placed; Object.fromEntries turns the map into the plain object the problem asks for.
